kid.question: What would happen to both large and small houses?

options.text: They would be abandoned
They would be plundered
They would be burned
They would be broken

kid.explanation: The Lord commands that the great house be struck with breaches and the little house with clefts.

kid.question: What did the people claim had given them power?

options.text: Their rulers' wisdom
Their own strength
Their allies' advice
Their priests' prayers

kid.explanation: They boast that they have taken horns, an image of power, by their own strength.

kid.question: What did the creatures in Amos's first vision eat?

options.text: The grass of the land
The grapes of the vineyard
The grain in the barns
The leaves of the orchard

kid.explanation: The grasshoppers are shown eating the grass, prompting Amos's plea for forgiveness.

kid.question: What did Amos ask after the first vision?

options.text: Lord, crown our king
Lord, enlarge our fields
Lord, please forgive
Lord, gather our troops

kid.explanation: Amos begs the Lord to forgive because Jacob is small; the Lord says the announced event will not be.

kid.question: What did the Lord hold while standing on the wall?

options.text: A sickle
A scroll
A plumbline
A sword

kid.explanation: The Lord stands on a wall with a plumbline and says He will set one amid Israel.

kid.question: What did Amaziah tell Amos to do?

options.text: Go to Judah and prophesy there
Go to Egypt and seek grain
Go to Edom and offer tribute
Go to Syria and seek allies

kid.explanation: Amaziah tells Amos to flee to Judah and forbids further prophecy at Bethel.

kid.question: Who had told Amos to prophesy to Israel?

options.text: The king
The Lord
The priest
The captain

kid.explanation: Amos says the Lord took him from following the flock and commissioned him to prophesy.

kid.question: What did Amos see in the next vision?

options.text: A jar of spring water
A bundle of dry branches
A bowl of crushed olives
A basket of summer fruit

kid.explanation: The Lord shows Amos a basket of summer fruit and announces the end upon Israel.

kid.question: What were the merchants planning when the Sabbath ended?

options.text: Seize vineyards by forging new deeds
Sell wheat with dishonest measures
Raise tolls at the city gates
Demand bribes from the village elders

kid.explanation: The merchants impatiently await the end of the Sabbath to sell wheat with dishonest measures.

kid.question: What did the Lord say about the oppressors' deeds?

options.text: He would tell them to priests
He would hide them from kings
He would never forget them
He would record them on walls

kid.explanation: The Lord swears that He will never forget their works.

high-school.question: What does the comparison with horses and plowing expose?

options.text: Justice has been delayed until after the next harvest
Farming has replaced military service for the poor
Justice has been changed into something poisonous
Farming has become the priests' main source of tribute

high-school.explanation: The questions about horses on rock and plowing lead into judgment turned to gall and righteousness's fruit to hemlock.

high-school.question: How does the next threat answer the boast about Israel's strength?

options.text: The Lord will transfer their cavalry to the priests
The Lord will raise a nation to afflict them
The Lord will divide their weapons among the poor
The Lord will require tribute from their royal guards

high-school.explanation: Their claim of power by their own strength is followed by the Lord raising an afflicting nation.

high-school.question: On what basis does Amos plead in the grasshopper and fire visions?

options.text: Jacob has paid the required temple tribute
Jacob is too small to rise unaided
Jacob has chosen a more faithful ruler
Jacob has already rebuilt the fallen sanctuaries

high-school.explanation: Both pleas ask how Jacob can rise because he is small; in both, the Lord relents.

high-school.question: How does the plumbline vision differ from the first two?

options.text: The Lord directs Amos to repeat his plea a third time
The Lord postpones action until the king completes a fast
The Lord accepts a royal gift in place of punishment
The Lord announces He will no longer pass by Israel

high-school.explanation: The first two visions end with 'It shall not be'; the plumbline vision instead announces no further passing by and ruined sanctuaries.

high-school.question: How does Amaziah present Amos's message to the king?

options.text: As a conspiracy the land cannot bear
As a rival claim to the throne
As a demand for higher royal tribute
As a threat against the ruler of Judah

high-school.explanation: Amaziah reports that Amos has conspired against Jeroboam and that the land cannot bear his words.

high-school.question: Why does Amaziah forbid prophecy at Bethel?

options.text: It is the place reserved for ancestral burials
It is the camp of the returning army
It is the king's sanctuary and court
It is the market reserved for foreign merchants

high-school.explanation: Amaziah grounds his prohibition in Bethel being the king's chapel and court.

high-school.question: How does Amos answer the attempt to send him away?

options.text: He grounds his mission in God's call from ordinary work
He grounds his mission in the king's earlier written invitation
He grounds his mission in the priests' request for sanctuary teaching
He grounds his mission in an inherited position at the court

high-school.explanation: Amos describes tending herds and gathering sycomore fruit, then the Lord taking him and commanding prophecy to Israel.

high-school.question: What does the summer-fruit vision announce about Israel's future?

options.text: An exile has ended, with temple songs welcoming returning families
A harvest has failed, with temple offerings moving to Judah
A siege has lifted, with temple priests resuming their duties
An end has arrived, with temple songs becoming howls

high-school.explanation: The basket is followed by 'The end is come' and temple songs turned to howlings amid many bodies.

high-school.question: Which market practices does Amos 8:5 combine?

options.text: Enlarging the grain measure and reducing the payment weight
Shrinking both the grain measure and the payment weight
Shrinking the grain measure and increasing the payment weight
Enlarging both the grain measure and the payment weight

high-school.explanation: A small ephah reduces the grain measure, a great shekel increases the payment, and false balances deepen the deceit.

high-school.question: How does the sale of wheat reveal exploitation beyond dishonest scales?

options.text: The traders tax foreign ships and confiscate their cargo
The traders buy needy people and sell inferior grain
The traders seize royal horses and charge rent for them
The traders close city wells and sell borrowed water

high-school.explanation: The accusation includes buying the poor for silver or shoes and selling the refuse of wheat.

expert.question: How does Amos 6:8-11 move from city to households?

options.text: The city is delivered up, then palaces are struck while small houses remain
The city pays tribute, then large and small houses receive returning captives
The city is delivered up, then large and small houses are struck
The city pays tribute, then palaces are emptied while small houses are struck

expert.explanation: The announced surrender of the city culminates in breaches for the great house and clefts for the little house.

expert.question: What relationship joins the boast of acquired 'horns' and the afflicting nation?

options.text: Claimed self-sufficiency is answered by divinely raised opposition
Claimed divine favor is answered by a newly appointed priesthood
Claimed royal ancestry is answered by the restoration of David's line
Claimed military defeat is answered by renewed foreign alliances

expert.explanation: Israel credits its own strength for its power; the Lord counters by raising a nation to afflict it throughout the stated territory.

expert.question: What is the structure shared by the first two visions of Amos 7?

options.text: Threatening vision, royal confession, and renewed covenant
Threatening vision, priestly offering, and military victory
Threatening vision, public migration, and restored harvest
Threatening vision, prophetic plea, and divine relenting

expert.explanation: Grasshoppers and fire each prompt Amos's plea over small Jacob, and the Lord says the threatened event will not occur.

expert.question: What shift marks the third vision's ending?

options.text: The relenting formulas give way to instructions for a national fast
The relenting formulas give way to an announced limit on forbearance
The intercessory speeches give way to a new promise of harvest
The intercessory speeches give way to a journey into foreign exile

expert.explanation: After two declarations that the event shall not be, the plumbline vision says the Lord will not pass by Israel anymore and names coming ruin.

expert.question: How should Amaziah's report about Jeroboam be distinguished from the preceding oracle?

options.text: Amaziah names the king's exile; the oracle names his death
Amaziah names the king's death; the oracle names his house
Amaziah names the city's burning; the oracle names its siege
Amaziah names the priest's death; the oracle names his family

expert.explanation: The Lord threatens the house of Jeroboam with the sword; Amaziah reports the message as Jeroboam dying by the sword.

expert.question: What competing grounds of authority emerge at Bethel?

options.text: Priestly descent at the shrine confronts a royal commission to collect tribute
Local election of the seer confronts an ancestral claim to the priesthood
Foreign control of the court confronts a treaty granting sanctuary access
Royal ownership of the shrine confronts a divine commission to speak

expert.explanation: Amaziah invokes the king's chapel and court; Amos answers with the Lord taking him from the flock and commanding prophecy.

expert.question: What grounds the personal sentence against Amaziah?

options.text: His command suppressing God's message is answered by a divine word
His demand increasing the tithe is answered by a priestly audit
His claim restoring the monarchy is answered by an ancestral genealogy
His treaty protecting foreign traders is answered by a royal decree

expert.explanation: 'Thou sayest, Prophesy not' is followed by 'Therefore thus saith the Lord' and announced calamity for Amaziah's household and Israel.

expert.question: What links the plumbline and summer-fruit visions through repeated language?

options.text: Both state that the Lord will send another prophet to Judah
Both state that the Lord will restore the altars before judgment
Both state that the Lord will no longer pass by His people
Both state that the Lord will gather the captives before harvest

expert.explanation: 'I will not again pass by them any more' occurs in both visions, marking a repeated limit on forbearance.

expert.question: What does the merchants' speech disclose about their religious calendar?

options.text: Observance interrupts commerce without displacing their intent to exploit
Observance provides a pretext for raising prices before the city assembles
Observance lets traders seize the grain set aside as temple offerings
Observance forces debtors to surrender fields instead of bringing sacrifices

expert.explanation: They await the new moon's and Sabbath's end in order to sell with false measures and buy the needy.

expert.question: How does the oath in Amos 8:7 answer the preceding commercial abuses?

options.text: The Lord delegates review of the offenders' accounts to the king
The Lord pledges enduring remembrance of the offenders' works
The Lord requires repayment before remembering the offenders' petitions
The Lord delays remembrance until the next festival gathering ends

expert.explanation: After detailing exploitation and deceit, the Lord swears that He will never forget any of their works.
